name: My Client's Case
title: My Client's Case

legal_basis.note: Parties must perform or offer to perform their respective promises

An admission is a statement suggesting an inference as to a fact in issue, and is evidence against the party who makes it. This restates the principle formerly in S.17 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872; the corresponding section of the Adhiniyam must be confirmed against the bare Act.

source: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023; Indian Contract Act, 1872
statutory_reference: Indian Contract Act, 1872 - S.37; Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 - section to be confirmed
authoring_note: The reply commits the client to a version of events. Anything asserted here will be put to the client in cross-examination and a departure from it is more damaging than a silence would have been, so the narration should be confined to what the client can prove from documents. Where a limitation, jurisdiction or arbitration objection is available, it should be taken in this reply rather than saved: a defence taken late invites the suggestion that it was an afterthought.
statute_currency: CITATION OUT OF DATE. The Indian Evidence Act, 1872 was repealed with effect from 1 July 2024 by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. The principle relied on here survives the repeal, but the SECTION NUMBER does not carry across - the Adhiniyam renumbered throughout. Published correspondence tables circulating online disagree with one another, so the advocate must map this citation against the bare Adhiniyam text rather than a table, and record the confirmed section here.
